title: Where Lab Time Goes: 6 Manual Tasks Scientists Can Stop Doing by Hand
summary: Six everyday manual lab tasks, the habit that fixes each one, and where a LIMS can take the task off the bench.
body_markdown:
A lot of lost lab time does not come from the experiments. It comes from the work around them: finding samples, moving numbers between files, and rebuilding what happened after the fact. Below are six manual lab tasks that eat scientists' days, the habit that fixes each one, and where lab software such as a LIMS can take the task off the bench entirely.


**Short answer:** the six biggest manual time sinks in a typical research or QC lab are hunting for samples, retyping instrument data, keeping spreadsheets in sync, rebuilding sample history, chasing signatures, and decoding labels and file names. Each one has a simple habit that helps today. Each one can also move into a connected system, so nobody has to do it by hand.


## 1. Hunting for boxes in the freezer


Someone needs one aliquot. The box was "top freezer, left side" when it went in. A while later, two people are holding the door open and reading frosted labels.


**Do this instead:** give every box an address and record it the moment the box goes in. Room, freezer, shelf, rack, box and position, written on the sample record, not on tape. When a box moves, the record moves with it.


**Where software helps:** in Scispot Location Manager, a digital twin of your rooms, freezers, shelves, racks and boxes, search finds racks and manifest boxes, and Assign location from a Labsheet records each sample in the box it sits in. Watch the 25-second tour:[Find any rack or box in Scispot Location Manager](https://youtube.com/shorts/h6q8HcysLFM) .


## 2. Retyping instrument data


The plate reader exports a file. Someone copies every value into a results sheet, checks a few by eye, and moves on. Every number copied by hand is one more chance for a typo, and nobody can say later which value came from where.


**Do this instead:** keep the raw export, untouched, next to the results. Move data by file, never by hand. Use the same export template every run so the columns are always in the same place.


**Where software helps:** Smart Actions, a Scibot skill in Scispot, runs every instrument file through the same steps. Upload the file (XLSX, XLS, CSV or XML), map wells to the samples on the plate manifest, apply your QC rules, then review the proposed results. Nothing is written until a scientist approves. Your lab builds the steps by dragging in rules and thresholds, with no code. See it in 25 seconds:[Stop retyping plate reader data](https://youtube.com/shorts/KjKXjAmA5tA) , or read more about[Smart Actions](https://www.scispot.com/smart-actions) .


## 3. Keeping spreadsheets in sync


Every lab has a spreadsheet only one person understands. It has merged cells, three date formats, and a yellow highlight that means "check this" to exactly one scientist. Then there is samples_final_v7_REAL.xlsx, and the copy someone saved to their desktop.


**Do this instead:** follow seven rules that keep a lab sheet readable after its author moves on.


The full set, with before-and-after examples, is available in a LinkedIn carousel.


**Where software helps:** a LIMS replaces the shared file with one record per sample. In Scispot, sample types, required fields, ID schemas, barcode labels, storage locations and ownership are defined up front, so every sample enters with the same context. See[Scispot LIMS](https://www.scispot.com/lims) .


## 4. Rebuilding sample history after the fact


An auditor, a collaborator or your own PI asks what happened to one sample. Answering means opening the intake sheet, the aliquot log, the freezer map, two instrument folders and an email thread.


**Do this instead:** record each step when it happens, with who, when and why. If a value changes, write the reason at the time of the change, not a week later.


**Where software helps:** in Scispot, sample lineage builds while the work happens. Aliquots, plates and slides inherit the parent sample's ID. Status changes, location moves and handoffs are logged with user, time and destination, and the next team is notified at handoff. Deletes ask for a reason and are recorded under the person who clicked delete ([25-second walkthrough](https://youtube.com/shorts/XSj81fnagj4) ). More on[sample traceability in Scispot](https://www.scispot.com/sample-traceability) .


## 5. Chasing signatures


A batch record waits on a QA signature. The analyst emails, then messages, then walks over. The reviewer did not know it was their turn.


**Do this instead:** agree on one review order for each record type, and one place every reviewer checks. Reviewers should know it is their turn without an email thread.


**Where software helps:** Scispot Home shows each reviewer the lab records that need their signature, whose turn it is in an ordered sign-off, and who a page is waiting on. Scispot supports 21 CFR Part 11 workflows, including ordered review and electronic signatures. Watch the[ELN sign-off walkthrough](https://youtu.be/Fqyy2LggaRI) .


## 6. Decoding labels and file names


"plate data FINAL (2).csv" and a tube that says "P4 HI" in marker. Six months later, neither means anything.


**Do this instead:** name files date first, then assay, plate, initials and version: 2026-11-26_ELISA_plate04_HI_v01.csv. Never call a file final. Give each sample one ID and print it on the label instead of writing it by hand.


**Where software helps:** setting up a sample ID and label convention? Try the[Scispot Lab Label Maker](https://www.scispot.com/lab-label-maker) .

## FAQ


### What are the most common time wasters in a research lab?


Searching for samples, copying instrument data by hand, reconciling spreadsheet versions, rebuilding sample history for a question or an audit, chasing reviewers for signatures, and decoding unclear labels and file names.


### How do I stop retyping instrument data?


Keep the raw export, use the same export template every run, and move data by file instead of by hand. In Scispot, Smart Actions, a Scibot skill, parses the instrument file, maps wells to samples, applies your QC rules and proposes results for review before anything is written.


### What is the best way to organize freezer samples?


Give every box an address (room, freezer, shelf, rack, box, position), record it on the sample record when the box goes in, and update it when the box moves. A digital freezer map such as Scispot Location Manager lets anyone search for a rack or box instead of opening doors.


### How do I keep a lab spreadsheet clean?


One row per sample, one ID column filled in every row, no merged cells, dates as YYYY-MM-DD, dropdowns for status, no meaning stored only in cell color, and raw data on its own tab that nobody edits.


### When does a lab need a LIMS instead of spreadsheets?


When more than one person edits the same sample data, when you need to show who changed what and when, when samples move between teams, or when audits and reviews depend on records being complete.


### Can Scispot work alongside an existing LIMS or spreadsheets?


Yes. Scispot can run alongside existing systems or replace spreadsheets where they create risk. Historical sample data can be migrated, and live records stay connected to the instruments, partners and reports that use them.
